strengths: Clear and well-motivated analysis: the paper provides empirical evidence (t-SNE token clustering, expert-subspace similarity measurements) that visual tokens' spatial redundancy and functional heterogeneity (conditional/unconditional under CFG) hinder expert specialization in vision MoE, directly grounding the method design in the diagnosis.

The two-step router (conditional routing for unconditional vs. conditional tokens, prototypical routing with learnable prototypes) is simple, sensible, and the semantic guidance validation (explicit classification-based vs. implicit k-means-based guidance in Tab. 1) convincingly supports the central claim that semantic routing guidance matters for vision MoE.

Comprehensive evaluation: four model sizes (S/B/L/XL) aligned with DiT, both DDPM and Rectified Flow objectives, CFG 1.0/1.5, comparisons against multiple recent MoE baselines (DiT-MoE, EC-DiT, DiffMoE) at matched activated parameters, plus scaling studies over model size, number of experts, activated experts, and training steps (up to 2M).

Substantial and consistent empirical gains: e.g., ProMoE-L-Flow FID 11.61/2.79 vs. Dense-DiT-XL-Flow 13.38/3.23, and clear improvements over DiffMoE-L with fewer total parameters; faster convergence shown via loss curves and cross-step comparisons (Tab. 10).

Thorough ablations: per-component (Tab. 6), activation function (Tab. 7), conditional routing portability to other routing schemes (Tab. 8), load-balancing loss interaction (Tab. 12), and RCL loss weight sensitivity (Tab. 13), plus detailed algorithm pseudocode supporting reproducibility.
weaknesses: Scope of validation is limited to class-conditional ImageNet 256×256; no text-to-image or higher-resolution experiments, so generality of the routing guidance to the settings where DiTs actually dominate (e.g., SD3-class text-to-image training) remains unverified.

Novelty is moderate: conditional routing is essentially a hand-crafted hard split by conditioning mask, and prototypical routing via cosine similarity to learnable prototypes is close to existing prototype/cluster-based routing ideas; the main novelty lies in the combination and the contrastive loss, which is a fairly standard InfoNCE-style objective applied to prototypes and token centroids.

Some baseline fairness concerns: MoE baselines are reimplemented and use different expert configurations (e.g., E8A1 vs. E14A1S1U1) and different total parameter counts; it is unclear how sensitive the comparison is to these hyperparameters, and the very large gains over baselines in Tab. 1 (5.91 vs. 8.22 FID) could partly reflect tuning differences.

Several design choices appear empirical/ad hoc without deeper justification, e.g., identity activation beating softmax (Tab. 7) is only argued informally; the claim that RCL acts as a load-balancing regularizer is supported only by an ablation without analysis of expert utilization statistics.

The claimed 'explicit semantic guidance' in the final method is actually implicit — RCL shapes prototypes using only routing statistics, so the headline framing slightly overstates what the final system does; also, no statistical variance or multiple-seed reporting for the main results.

The unconditional-expert mechanism interacts with CFG inference in ways that could change the effective compute/behavior at inference versus baselines (extra unconditional expert not counted in the activated-parameter framing is discussed but only briefly).

strengths: Well-motivated analysis of why MoE underperforms in DiTs: the language-vs-visual token comparison (Fig. 1a, extended in Appendix C.1) and expert-subspace similarity measurement (Fig. 1b) provide a concrete, quantified diagnosis rather than pure conjecture.

Comprehensive experimental protocol: four model scales (S/B/L/XL), two training objectives (DDPM and Rectified Flow), comparisons against multiple MoE baselines (DiT-MoE, EC-DiT, DiffMoE) under matched activated parameters, and additional training-step comparisons (Tab. 10).

Reasonably thorough ablations: component-wise (Tab. 6), activation function (Tab. 7), conditional routing applied to another routing scheme (Tab. 8), load-balancing interaction (Tab. 12), loss weight sensitivity (Tab. 13), expert count scaling, and top-k activation (Tab. 11).
Consistent and sizable FID/IS improvements over both dense DiT and MoE baselines, plus qualitative samples and t-SNE token-assignment visualizations supporting the expert-specialization claims.
Transparent reporting, including a limitations section, ethics/reproducibility statements, and detailed Algorithm 1.
weaknesses: Limited conceptual novelty. The three components are individually simple and largely assembled from known ideas: hard routing on conditioning type is a hand-crafted shortcut; prototype-based routing via cosine similarity is a standard mechanism; RCL is essentially an InfoNCE-style objective over prototypes and batch centroids. The framing ('explicit routing guidance') oversells what are fairly straightforward design choices.

Internal results undercut the central contribution. In Tab. 1, the simple classification-based routing (FID 5.91) and k-means-based routing (6.24) both outperform the full proposed ProMoE (6.39) at cfg=1.5. This suggests the main gain comes from 'any semantic guidance' rather than the specific proposed RCL/prototype mechanism, weakening the significance of the proposed method over cheaper alternatives.

Conditional routing may be a near-trivial trick. Unconditional tokens are deterministically identifiable from the conditioning flag, and the unconditional expert is unused at inference without CFG; it is unclear this constitutes 'routing' in any meaningful sense versus simply adding a dedicated FFN branch, and the ablation isolating it (Tab. 6) shows the smallest effect.

Scope of validation is narrow: only class-conditional ImageNet 256×256. The 'semantic' prototypes are presumably encouraged to align with the 1K class structure, so generalization to text-to-image or other conditioning regimes—where the motivation about semantic specialization would matter most—is untested and uncertain.

Fairness concerns in baseline comparisons: all MoE baselines are self-implemented and trained under the authors' settings at a fixed 500K steps; ProMoE uses 14 experts vs. 8 for baselines, and the extra unconditional/shared expert structure changes the architecture beyond routing. Baselines being potentially under-tuned cannot be ruled out.

The motivating analysis is partly anecdotal and circular: Fig. 1(b) compares expert diversity of DiT-MoE vs. the authors' own method, and the t-SNE/k-means distance-ratio statistics are coarse proxies that conflate spatial redundancy with semantic clustering without a rigorous causal link to MoE performance.

Several claims lack direct evidence, e.g., that identity activation 'enables direct top-K selection and provides stable training' is asserted from a single empirical ablation without analysis; the claim that RCL's push-away term acts as load balancing is supported only by observing that adding a load-balancing loss slightly hurts.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem analysis: the paper provides quantitative evidence (Fig. 1, Appendix C.1) that visual tokens exhibit high spatial redundancy and functional heterogeneity (conditional vs. unconditional under CFG), which plausibly explains why MoE gains in DiTs lag behind LLMs. This diagnostic framing is a genuine strength.

The proposed two-step router (conditional routing + prototypical routing) and the routing contrastive loss are simple, well-specified, and directly address the diagnosed issues; Algorithm 1 makes the method easy to reimplement.

Comprehensive and largely fair evaluation: comparisons against Dense DiT, DiT-MoE, EC-DiT, and DiffMoE at matched activated parameters and comparable total parameters, across four model sizes (S/B/L/XL) and both DDPM and Rectified Flow objectives.

Strong empirical results: consistent FID/IS improvements over dense and MoE baselines (e.g., ProMoE-L-Flow 11.61/2.79 vs. Dense-DiT-XL-Flow 13.38/3.23), faster convergence, and gains over baselines trained with more steps and more total parameters (Tab. 10, DiffMoE with 1.846B params).

Thorough ablations: each component (prototypical routing, RCL, conditional routing), activation function choice, load-balancing loss interplay, loss weight sensitivity, number of experts, and number of activated experts are all studied.
Good reproducibility practices: public benchmark, promised code and weights, detailed implementation settings, and an explicit LLM-usage statement.
weaknesses: Scope of validation is narrow: all experiments are class-conditional ImageNet 256x256 generation with FID/IS only. There is no text-to-image or higher-resolution evaluation, which is where modern DiTs (and the claimed scalability motivation) actually matter; the paper itself acknowledges this in the limitations section.

The conditional-routing component is tightly coupled to the CFG training paradigm (hard-splitting tokens by null vs. specific conditioning). Its generalization to text-to-image models, where conditioning is heterogeneous and 'unconditional' tokens arise differently, is untested and questionable, limiting the claimed broad relevance of the framework.

Limited technical novelty: prototypical/cosine-similarity routing, shared experts, fine-grained expert segmentation, and contrastive losses on centroids are all established components; the contribution is primarily their combination and adaptation to DiT-MoE rather than a fundamentally new mechanism.

Gains under the DDPM objective at the B scale are marginal (41.19 -> 40.37 FID at cfg=1.0), so the method's benefit is not uniformly strong across settings; most headline gains come from Rectified Flow.

Some design choices are justified only empirically without deeper analysis, e.g., identity activation outperforming softmax/sigmoid is reported but underexplored; the interaction between RCL's push-away term and load balancing is characterized only through ablations.

FID/IS at 500K steps are relatively early checkpoints; while extended-step results are provided for a subset of models, baselines are not always trained to full convergence in every comparison, which slightly complicates the strength of the SOTA claims.

Expert-diversity analysis (Fig. 1b) and t-SNE assignment visualizations (Fig. 6) are suggestive but largely qualitative; a more rigorous quantification of expert specialization and its causal link to FID gains would strengthen the central claim that 'routing matters'.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper provides a concrete analysis (t-SNE clustering statistics in Fig. 1 and Appendix C) of why visual tokens differ from language tokens (spatial redundancy, functional heterogeneity from CFG), and ties this analysis directly to the design of the method.

The proposed two-step router (conditional routing separating unconditional/conditional tokens, followed by prototypical routing with learnable prototypes) is simple, well-specified (Algorithm 1), and the routing contrastive loss is label-free, supporting top-K assignment, and doubles as a load-balancing regularizer, which is validated in Table 17.

Comprehensive and fairly conducted evaluation: comparisons against dense DiT and multiple MoE baselines (DiT-MoE, EC-DiT, DiffMoE, GMM-based routing) under both Rectified Flow and DDPM objectives at matched activated parameters and comparable total parameters, with FLOPs, training time, and inference time reported (Table 14) to rule out computational confounds.

Extensive ablations (component-wise, activation function, conditional routing within K-means routing, loss weight, number of experts, load-balancing loss), scaling studies across model sizes (S/B/L/XL) and expert counts, extended training comparisons up to 2M steps, and a text-to-image GenEval experiment demonstrating generalization beyond class-conditional ImageNet.

Honest limitations section (metric limitations) and a reproducibility statement with code/weights promised; expert utilization analysis (Fig. 6) provides qualitative evidence that the method actually induces specialization rather than just improving FID.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate: cosine-similarity routing against learnable prototypes and contrastive-style routing losses build on well-established ideas (shared experts, DeepSeek-style fine-grained experts, prototype-based assignment, contrastive clustering); the main conceptual novelty is the conditional/unconditional token split, which is somewhat CFG-specific and may not generalize to architectures or training regimes where the conditional/unconditional distinction is less clean (e.g., distillation, guidance-free models).

The empirical scope is narrow in terms of tasks: the core results are class-conditional ImageNet 256x256; the text-to-image experiment is small-scale (2M LAION subset, 400K steps, a 3B model, GenEval only, no FID or comparison with established T2I systems), so claims of generalization to realistic generative settings are only lightly supported.

The motivating analysis is largely empirical/anecdotal (t-SNE plots, cluster distance ratios on sampled tokens); there is no quantitative characterization of how routing failure modes arise, and no theoretical grounding for why cosine similarity with identity activation is the right inductive bias (the softmax-vs-identity choice is resolved empirically only).

Some baselines are missing or recent-but-uncompared: Expert Race (Yuan et al., 2025) is cited and discussed but not compared; comparisons with other guidance-aware routing or timestep-aware MoE methods (e.g., RMoE, Switch-DiT, LanteFlow) are absent despite being cited.

Potential fairness concerns in Table 5: ProMoE uses 14 experts vs. 8 for baselines and a different expert configuration (shared + unconditional experts); although activated parameters and FLOPs are matched, the benefit of the extra unconditional expert alone is not fully disentangled from the prototypical routing contribution at the L scale.

Hard routing of unconditional tokens to a single dedicated expert could create a train/inference mismatch when CFG configurations vary at inference; the paper tests only CFG in {1.0, 1.5, 4.0} and does not analyze robustness to distribution shift in the conditional/unconditional token ratio.

strengths: Clear and well-motivated problem framing: the paper provides an empirical analysis (t-SNE cluster separation, expert subspace similarity) of why MoE transfers poorly from LLMs to DiTs, attributing the gap to visual-token redundancy and conditional/unconditional functional heterogeneity.

The proposed two-step router is simple but sensible: hard-splitting unconditional tokens to dedicated experts is a direct, well-targeted fix for CFG-induced functional heterogeneity, and prototype-based routing is a natural way to inject semantic structure.

Very comprehensive empirical validation: results across three model scales (B/L/XL), both DDPM and Rectified Flow objectives, with and without CFG, comparisons against dense DiT and multiple MoE baselines (DiT-MoE, EC-DiT, DiffMoE) under matched activated parameters, plus 2M-step extended training comparisons.

Thorough ablation studies: component-wise ablations (Table 7), activation function choice (Table 8), load-balancing loss interaction (Table 17), RCL loss weight sensitivity (Table 18), expert-count scaling, and k-means/GMM-based routing alternatives.

Extra analyses strengthen the case: expert utilization visualization (Fig. 6), training loss convergence (Fig. 5), GFLOPs/training/inference-time cost comparisons (Table 14), and a small-scale text-to-image experiment on GenEval showing generalization beyond class-conditional ImageNet.
Reproducibility is well supported: detailed hyperparameters, pseudocode (Algorithm 1), and a commitment to releasing code and weights.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate. Prototype/cosine-similarity routing is essentially a linear router with normalized weights, and the conditional/unconditional expert split is a fairly direct engineering consequence of CFG; neither component is technically deep. The routing contrastive loss is a standard prototype-pull/push objective, and its role overlaps substantially with conventional load balancing (the paper itself notes this in Table 17).

The motivating analysis in Fig. 1 is somewhat anecdotal: t-SNE visualizations and a single inter-/intra-class distance ratio on 110 classes do not constitute rigorous evidence that token redundancy is the cause of MoE underperformance in DiTs; the causal link is asserted more than established.

Gains may be partially attributable to capacity rather than routing design: ProMoE uses notably more total parameters than dense baselines (e.g., 1.568B vs 675M activated) and slightly more than some MoE baselines in certain settings; while activated-parameter matching is provided, a dense model matched on total parameters is not compared.

Evaluation is confined to class-conditional ImageNet 256×256 and a small-scale (2M-subset LAION, 400K steps) text-to-image experiment. There is no evaluation at higher resolutions or on modern large-scale T2I settings where MoE scaling claims matter most, and metrics are limited to FID/IS, which the authors themselves acknowledge in the limitations.

The main tables report only 500K training steps for headline comparisons; although extended-step comparisons exist in the appendix, the main-text results sit in a regime where MoE methods are known to lag and where the claimed advantages might compress at full training budgets (the 2M-step results partially address this but gains narrow).

Some design choices feel under-justified: identity activation for router scores is argued mainly empirically, the hard conditional/unconditional split raises questions about behavior when CFG is disabled or when conditioning is continuous text (only briefly addressed for the small T2I experiment), and no variance/error bars are reported for FID results.

strengths: The paper is well motivated: the analysis of differences between language and visual tokens (semantic density, spatial redundancy, conditional/unconditional functional heterogeneity) provides a clear, testable hypothesis for why MoE underperforms in DiTs, and the motivating experiments (Fig. 1, appendix C.1-C.2) are a nice touch.

The proposed two-step router is clearly described: hard conditional/unconditional partitioning plus prototypical cosine-similarity routing with a routing contrastive loss is a coherent design, and the ablations (Tables 7-9, 17-18) show each component contributes.

Evaluation is unusually thorough for this area: comparisons against dense DiT and three MoE baselines (DiT-MoE, EC-DiT, DiffMoE) under both DDPM and Rectified Flow objectives, across four model sizes (S/B/L/XL), multiple CFG scales, expert-count scaling, extended training up to 2M steps, computational cost accounting (Table 14), expert-utilization analysis, and an initial text-to-image experiment (GenEval).

Gains are consistent and non-trivial: e.g., ProMoE-L surpasses DiffMoE-L and even larger total-parameter baselines at matched activated parameters, and the paper reports fair activated/total parameter accounting throughout.
Reproducibility appears good: implementation details, hyperparameters, an algorithm box, public baselines, and a code/weights release promise are included; limitations and LLM usage are disclosed.
weaknesses: Novelty is moderate rather than groundbreaking. Individual components build on well-known ideas: shared/unconditional experts follow DeepSeek-MoE-style designs, prototype/cosine routing resembles prior prototype-based routers, and the contrastive loss is a fairly direct adaptation. The main contribution is the combination plus the empirical insight that explicit semantic guidance matters for vision MoE.

The absolute generation quality remains modest: main results are at 500K steps (FID ~8-12 at XL), well short of published DiT-XL/2 numbers (FID 2.27 at 7M steps). The 2M-step appendix results help, but the headline comparisons are at a training regime where all methods are far from convergence, which somewhat weakens claims of superiority.

The benchmark scope is narrow: essentially all quantitative evidence is class-conditional ImageNet. The text-to-image experiment is small-scale (2M LAION subset, 400K steps, 3B activated) with no comparison to established T2I baselines, so generality beyond ImageNet is only weakly supported. It is also unclear how the batch-level CFG conditional/unconditional partition transfers to token-level text conditioning settings typical of modern T2I models.

A potential confound deserves more scrutiny: the strongest guidance variant (classification-based routing, Table 1) uses the same class labels as the conditioning signal, so gains could partly come from injecting the conditioning information into routing rather than from generic 'semantic guidance.' The ablation showing routing-classification guidance helps even without load balancing partially addresses this, but a cleaner disentangling experiment (e.g., guidance from an external signal, or guidance on unconditional-only data) would strengthen the causal claim.

The gating design (identity activation, unnormalized top-K scores, no softmax) is justified only empirically and briefly; a theoretical or at least deeper empirical discussion of stability/gradient behavior would help. Similarly, the quantitative basis of the token-redundancy analysis (Fig. 1a) is a single k-means distance ratio on randomly sampled tokens, which is suggestive but fragile.

The t-SNE 'well-formed clusters' visualizations (Fig. 7, C.2) are qualitative and could be subject to confirmation bias; quantitative cluster-quality metrics would make the expert-specialization claims more rigorous.
